near_miss.lead: MIr. tír fhliuch thirim (*ters- + *wleikʷ-) ~ Lat. terra + liquor
near_miss.why_not: Irish is an oxymoronic land-description (wet/dry, pleasant/unpleasant) list; Lucretius pairs the elements earth and water in cosmology. The cognate roots are real, but the contexts differ and 'earth and water' is generic; no shared figure.
Irish: charioteer releases the river-dam (scaoilis an chora... an sruth); OE: sea-currents eddy against the beach. Common word, no shared collocation.

near_miss.lead: breast/belly + heart: MIr. broind (brú) ... cride i clíab ~ ON brjóst ... hjarta
near_miss.why_not: Irish is a stock TBC wound-run (repeated verbatim at mga:G301035:#1/11:15): spear through the shield over the belly, breaks three ribs, pierces the heart in the chest. ON contexts are Þorkell's heart quaking in his breast, a skaldic 'heart did not quake in the breast', and a love passage. Breast and heart co-occur everywhere; no shared figure.

near_miss.lead: ice imagery in battle: MIr. bommanna ega 'lumps (hailstones) of ice' ~ OE hilde-gicelum 'battle-icicles' (*h₁yeg-)
near_miss.why_not: Fergus boasts the severed heads would be as many as lumps of ice (a counting simile, cf. the full unit in units.jsonl); Beowulf's sword melts into icicles in battle-blood. Same root, different figure; ice/hail images in battle are common.

near_miss.lead: milk + cow: MIr. bó ... bleaghain ~ ON mjólka kýr (*h₂melǵ- + *gʷōws)
near_miss.why_not: Everyday collocation; Irish is a list of tribute cattle ('milch cows'), Grettir is a housewife milking. Generic, no formulaic context.

near_miss.lead: wood + root: ON rótum ... viðar, OE wudu wyrtum fæst
near_miss.why_not: Germanic-internal only; the Irish pivot has no 'root' (rena = ré n-a 'before their'); Ulstermen clearing a wood with swords before their chariots.

near_miss.lead: father and mother pairs (athair/máthair, pitā mātā, faðir)
near_miss.why_not: Kinship pair is universal; contexts unrelated (boy raised in his parents' house; charm genealogy; Lucretius on recognition).
Irish: the noise of the monster cat Irusán approaching like thunder; the partners are the god's name and a drum charm. Shared root only.

near_miss.lead: colour + horse: MIr. ech líath ~ ON fölvan jó
near_miss.why_not: Irish is the description of Cú Chulainn's grey chariot horse in a long adjectival run; Edda has Helgi's pale horse on the sky-road. 'Grey/pale horse' is generic, and líath is not secure as a *pelH- derivative (more likely *(p)leyto-), so the colour words may not be cognate.

near_miss.lead: father/mother; AVŚ dyauḥ pitā pṛthivī mātā
near_miss.why_not: Only the kinship terms are shared; no Celtic or Norse counterpart of the sky-father/earth-mother pair in these passages; Irish is a welcome 'for your mother's and father's sake'.

near_miss.lead: heroic heat: Cú Chulainn's body-heat melting snow ~ blood so hot it melts the sword
near_miss.why_not: Thematic parallel (battle-heat), but no cognate wording: MIr. bruth (*bʰrewh₁-) and OE forbarn/hāt are different roots.

near_miss.lead: negated flight + foot/track: MIr. ní rugus troigh teithidh 'I never took a foot of flight' ~ Serb. да од врага не утече трага 'that not a trace escape from the enemy' (*tregʰ- + *tekʷ-)
near_miss.why_not: The pair of roots really is shared (Ir. traig ~ PSl. *tragъ < *tregʰ-; teichid ~ uteći < *tekʷ-), but the Serbian line is a one-off variant of the rhymed formula да од врага не остане/остаје трага (c. 15 hits in Vuk, with 'remain'), and the meanings differ (a hero who never retreats vs. annihilating the enemy). The Irish idiom troigh theithid is late (Early Modern annals, late TBC recension).

near_miss.lead: father/mother + hero driven from his land: MIr. máthair athair ... indarb át chrích ~ Skt pitrā mātrā ... vīro nirvāsyate
near_miss.why_not: Superficially congruent (exiling a warrior from his land), but the Irish is a reproach-catalogue and the only shared cognates are kinship words and fer/vīra; no shared phrase.

near_miss.lead: take a spit: MIr. bior ... do ghabhail ~ Umbr. hahtu berus (*gʷeru-)
near_miss.why_not: bior ~ berus is an exact cognate, but taking or putting food on spits is everyday kitchen and ritual language, and the verbs (gaibid vs. hahtu) are not securely cognate.

near_miss.lead: healing waters: wounds washed in the streams/rivers (srotha, aibnib) ~ āpaḥ ... susruvur ... muñcantu aṃhasaḥ
near_miss.why_not: Thematic (healing or releasing waters), but the shared root *srew- 'flow' is generic with water, and MIr. ab/aub (*abon-) is not the same stem as Skt ap-.

error.correct_reading: ré n-a 'before their' (prep. ré + 3pl possessive), rena carpdib 'before their chariots'
error.evidence: Context: Ulstermen cutting the wood with their swords before their chariots; not fren 'root'.

error.correct_reading: uirthi (prep. pron. 'on it, fem.'), edition uirt[h]i; gabhois uirthi
error.evidence: Bracketed letter split the form; it is ar + 3sg fem., not orcaid.

error.correct_reading: brú 'belly', dat. broinn (scíath ósa broind 'the shield over his belly'); generally connected with Gmc *breust- 'breast' (*bʰrews- 'swell')
error.evidence: Same form recurs at mga:G301035:#1/11:15. (Etymology recalled.)

error.correct_reading: buinne 'torrent, gush, outburst' here (amhail buinne teinedh 'like a gush of fire'); not 'bind'
error.evidence: Context is a simile of fire; the *bʰendʰ- link fits neither this sense nor the 'bracelet' homograph securely.
